title: Generative “AI”: The Guitar Hero of Creativity

content_html:
Posted on August 6, 2026    Posted by      49 Comments

So, you’re a person who has decided to embark on a creative journey of self-expression — to make art, in other words. First off, this is awesome! The universe needs more people making art, whether that art is writing, painting, music or any other form that humans are capable of creating. You have the drive, now all you need is to find an instrument. Will it be a guitar? A pen? A paint brush? A camera? Yarn for fiber art? What will you choose to take those first steps into a larger creative world?

What? You say you’re just going to type prompts into a generative “AI” interface? After all, with a single sentence, generative “AI” can plop out something that seems passably like human-created music, or writing, or illustration, or whatever. It’s super-easy to use and results, at least at first glance, look… pretty good! It seems like an effective way to jump into a creative life, no?

Well… there are lots of counter-arguments creative people might make to this (not the least of which is that prompting a generative “AI” makes one an artist exactly as much as pushing a button on an automated hotel pancake maker makes one a chef), but let me attempt a metaphor that I think works pretty well:

Remember Guitar Hero? It was a really cool rhythm video game where a player, armed with a special guitar-shaped button controller, would pick a song, and then press the buttons, singly or in combination, in time to visual cues on a screen. You got points for hitting buttons at the correct time, and for doing that lots of times in a row. It was fun and at higher levels you could absolutely give your fingers a workout — let’s face it, if you could get through the entire of “Through the Fire and Flames” on expert level, you were a friggin’ god.

What you weren’t was a guitar player.

That’s because nothing about Guitar Hero taught you how to play guitar — what it taught you was how to use the guitar-shaped controller for the game. Was it a skill pressing the buttons at the right time? Yes! But it was a non-transferrable skill that had no application for the actual musical instrument. The game’s gameplay mechanic doesn’t map to the mechanics of a guitar in any meaningful sense; it doesn’t teach you scales or chords or how to put them together in new and unexpected ways to create something original. All you could do with Guitar Hero was use the controller in the way the game-makers wanted you to, in time with the songs they chose, to accrue points and achievements that they specified.

Sure, it’s all gamified and fun and even addictive, but at the end of the day no outside, transferable skill accrues to the player. To do that, you have to set the controller down, pick up an actual guitar, and start another, entirely different journey. And perhaps some Guitar Hero player did or will, which is awesome. It means at some point they were not satisfied with pretending to play the guitar, following someone else’s rules and set-up. They still started, effectively, at zero. There was a whole new skill tree to be learned that had very little to do with the game, outside of the shape of the controller.

Being a Guitar Hero player did not — and does not! — equal being a guitar player.

So, let’s come back to “AI,” which in this case is “generative ‘AI,'” the sort which powers most consumer-facing “AI” like ChatGPT or Gemini or Claude or Grok. Like Guitar Hero, generative “AI” has a vast database of artist’s work to draw from (but unlike Guitar Hero, whose makers licensed that work and compensated the musicians and songwriters, most generative “AI” training data is pirated and uncompensated). Like Guitar Hero, generative “AI” is programmed by its makers; its outputs are to a greater or lesser extent shaped by those makers through algorithms and weights, which is why Anthropic’s Claude “AI” has a different “personality” than say, “Grok,” and why “AI” text and images have a particular tone and texture which is easy enough to clock when you see enough of it. Like Guitar Hero, “AI” is fun to play with and the results, again, at least superficially, can be pretty cool. A well-tuned prompt can create some initially impressive results.

But, like Guitar Hero, no outside creative skill has been acquired or developed. Every result is self-contained within the domain of a program whose owners have their own goals and agenda, and to whom nearly every benefit accrues. Material generated by “AI” can’t be owned by the prompter if it is purely generated by the “AI,” and even partial “AI” generation in a work raises legal concerns regarding rights and ownership. In a very real sense “AI” can’t even be directly controlled — prompting is an interface with the underlying weights and algorithms of the “AI,” chosen and directed by others. The more granular the prompting, the more the underlying “AI” can use its weights and algorithms to fulfill the request, but at the end of the day, you still get what you get. If it’s not exactly what you wanted you have to hope another prompt will get it closer. You keep pressing the button on the automated pancake maker, hoping it will make exactly the pancake you want.

Prompting, like playing with the Guitar Hero controller, doesn’t teach you how to do anything else. Prompting doesn’t give one the eventual skill to sit at a keyboard and write a short story or a novel. It doesn’t give one the ability to play a musical instrument. It doesn’t let you pick up a pen and create a drawing. The skill required for all of those — not to mention the life experience to create meaning with them — lives somewhere else. When you’re using “AI,” you can’t get there from here. You have to start again from zero. The time you spent in “AI” doesn’t count for this, except in the very limited sense of showing you what you don’t want.

Just like being good at Guitar Hero does not make one a guitar player, being able to prompt doesn’t easily make one a creator. At best, it tells what is essentially a statistical engine what you want it to output based on the vast database of other people’s work that it is drawing from. Nothing it cobbles together gives you the experience of creation; the only benefit of that crank of the “AI” flywheel is to the company that owns the “AI.” The image or music or video or text is not from you, it’s just something you asked for. You’re not the creator. You are, perhaps, the creator’s manager.

And, look, for some people that’s enough! There is a reason why legions of Facebookers flood their feeds with images and video of “AI” cats (and why, rather less adorably, legions of bots flood those same feeds with fake images of people their prompters want you to hate). Lots of people don’t want to be “creative” in any meaningful sense of the world, they just want those images of cats having coffee or whatever. Not everyone who played Guitar Hero wanted to actually play guitar, either. That’s fine (well, for Guitar Hero. “AI” has resource and rights issues to deal with no matter how it’s used. But I trust we all understand where I’m going here).

But if you want to create, it helps to create. You can’t just prompt your way into it. You have to do it. You have to learn and work and build skills and ability. You have to be bad at it before you can be good at it. Your creativity has to be inherent and portable, something you carry with you wherever you go, not contingent on a service provided by billionaires who have their finger on the scale of how that service does its thing.

Because, among any other thing, who is to say how long any of these “AI” are going to be around? The last installment of Guitar Hero came out more than a decade ago. The online version of the game shut down in 2020. Everyone who ever had mad skills on Guitar Hero has had those skills out to pasture for a while now. Now, apparently there’s going to be an updated version of the Guitar Hero concept later this year, which is cool and I hope is as much fun as the previous version. We’ll see how long it lasts. Meanwhile, as long as their fingers and shoulders hold out, everyone who ever learned guitar still has those skills and the ability to use them.

So, keep that in mind as your start your journey of self-expression. You have a whole bunch of paths you can go down here. Some will be harder and take more time than others. But those are the ones that are more likely to get you to where you want to go, to develop the skills and abilities to let you say what you want to say, how you want to say it, without having to rely on anyone or anything else, to make it happen. Your choice! Pick well.

— JS

sentences.zh: 与《吉他英雄》一样，生成“AI”拥有庞大的艺术家作品数据库可供借鉴（但与《吉他英雄》不同的是，《吉他英雄》的制作者获得了作品许可并向音乐家和词曲作者提供补偿，大多数生成“AI”训练数据都是盗版且无偿的）。

sentences.en: Like Guitar Hero, generative “AI” is programmed by its makers; its outputs are to a greater or lesser extent shaped by those makers through algorithms and weights, which is why Anthropic’s Claude “AI” has a different “personality” than say, “Grok,” and why “AI” text and images have a particular tone and texture which is easy enough to clock when you see enough of it.
sentences.zh: 与《吉他英雄》一样，生成“AI”是由其制作者编程的；它的输出或多或少是由那些制造者通过算法和权重塑造的，这就是为什么 Anthropic 的 Claude “AI” 具有与“Grok”不同的“个性”，也是为什么“AI”文本和图像具有特定的色调和纹理，当你看到足够多的时候，很容易就能识别出来。

sentences.en: Like Guitar Hero, “AI” is fun to play with and the results, again, at least superficially, can be pretty cool.
sentences.zh: 就像《吉他英雄》一样，“AI”玩起来很有趣，而且结果也很酷，至少表面上是这样。

sentences.en: A well-tuned prompt can create some initially impressive results.
sentences.zh: 精心调整的提示可以创造一些最初令人印象深刻的结果。

blocks.html_en: But, like Guitar Hero, no outside creative skill has been acquired or developed. Every result is self-contained within the domain of a program whose owners have their own goals and agenda, and to whom nearly every benefit accrues. Material generated by “AI” can’t be owned by the prompter if it is purely generated by the “AI,” and even partial “AI” generation in a work raises legal concerns regarding rights and ownership. In a very real sense “AI” can’t even be directly controlled — prompting is an interface with the underlying weights and algorithms of the “AI,” chosen and directed by others. The more granular the prompting, the more the underlying “AI” can use its weights and algorithms to fulfill the request, but at the end of the day, you still get what you get. If it’s not exactly what you wanted you have to hope another prompt will get it closer. You keep pressing the button on the automated pancake maker, hoping it will make exactly the pancake you want.

sentences.en: You keep pressing the button on the automated pancake maker, hoping it will make exactly the pancake you want.
sentences.zh: 你不断地按下自动煎饼机上的按钮，希望它能做出你想要的煎饼。

blocks.html_en: Prompting, like playing with the Guitar Hero controller, doesn’t teach you how to do anything else. Prompting doesn’t give one the eventual skill to sit at a keyboard and write a short story or a novel. It doesn’t give one the ability to play a musical instrument. It doesn’t let you pick up a pen and create a drawing. The skill required for all of those — not to mention the life experience to create meaning with them — lives somewhere else. When you’re using “AI,” you can’t get there from here. You have to start again from zero. The time you spent in “AI” doesn’t count for this, except in the very limited sense of showing you what you don’t want.

blocks.html_en: Just like being good at Guitar Hero does not make one a guitar player, being able to prompt doesn’t easily make one a creator. At best, it tells what is essentially a statistical engine what you want it to output based on the vast database of other people’s work that it is drawing from. Nothing it cobbles together gives you the experience of creation; the only benefit of that crank of the “AI” flywheel is to the company that owns the “AI.” The image or music or video or text is not from you, it’s just something you asked for. You’re not the creator. You are, perhaps, the creator’s manager.

blocks.html_en: And, look, for some people that’s enough! There is a reason why legions of Facebookers flood their feeds with images and video of “AI” cats (and why, rather less adorably, legions of bots flood those same feeds with fake images of people their prompters want you to hate). Lots of people don’t want to be “creative” in any meaningful sense of the world, they just want those images of cats having coffee or whatever. Not everyone who played Guitar Hero wanted to actually play guitar, either. That’s fine (well, for Guitar Hero. “AI” has resource and rights issues to deal with no matter how it’s used. But I trust we all understand where I’m going here).

sentences.en: But I trust we all understand where I’m going here).

blocks.html_en: But if you want to create, it helps to create. You can’t just prompt your way into it. You have to do it. You have to learn and work and build skills and ability. You have to be bad at it before you can be good at it. Your creativity has to be inherent and portable, something you carry with you wherever you go, not contingent on a service provided by billionaires who have their finger on the scale of how that service does its thing.

blocks.html_en: Because, among any other thing, who is to say how long any of these “AI” are going to be around? The last installment of Guitar Hero came out more than a decade ago. The online version of the game shut down in 2020. Everyone who ever had mad skills on Guitar Hero has had those skills out to pasture for a while now. Now, apparently there’s going to be an updated version of the Guitar Hero concept later this year, which is cool and I hope is as much fun as the previous version. We’ll see how long it lasts. Meanwhile, as long as their fingers and shoulders hold out, everyone who ever learned guitar still has those skills and the ability to use them.

blocks.html_en: So, keep that in mind as your start your journey of self-expression. You have a whole bunch of paths you can go down here. Some will be harder and take more time than others. But those are the ones that are more likely to get you to where you want to go, to develop the skills and abilities to let you say what you want to say, how you want to say it, without having to rely on anyone or anything else, to make it happen. Your choice! Pick well.

content_html_zh:
发表于 八月 6, 2026 发表者 49 条评论

所以，你是一个决定踏上自我表达的创造性旅程的人——换句话说，就是创作艺术。 首先，这太棒了！ 宇宙需要更多的人创作艺术，无论艺术是写作、绘画、音乐还是人类能够创造的任何其他形式。 你已经有了动力，现在你所需要的就是找到一个工具。 它会是一把吉他吗？ 一支笔？ 画笔？ 相机？ 纤维艺术用纱线？ 您会选择什么来迈出进入更大创意世界的第一步？

什么？ 你说你只是要在生成的“AI”界面中输入提示？ 毕竟，只需一句话，生成式“人工智能”就可以生成一些看起来还过得去的东西，比如人类创造的音乐、写作、插图或其他东西。 它非常易于使用和结果，至少乍一看，看起来...... 不错！ 这似乎是进入创意生活的有效方式，不是吗？

出色地… 创意人士可能会对此提出很多反驳意见（其中最重要的是，促使生成“人工智能”使一个人成为艺术家，就像按下自动酒店煎饼机上的按钮使一个人成为厨师一样），但让我尝试一个我认为非常有效的比喻：

还记得《吉他英雄》吗？ 这是一款非常酷的节奏视频游戏，玩家配备一个特殊的吉他形状的按钮控制器，可以选择一首歌曲，然后根据屏幕上的视觉提示，单独或组合按下按钮。 在正确的时间按下按钮并连续多次按下按钮即可获得积分。 这很有趣，在更高的水平上，你绝对可以锻炼你的手指——让我们面对现实吧，如果你能在专家水平上完成整个“穿越火焰”，你就是一个该死的上帝。

你不是吉他手。

这是因为《吉他英雄》并没有教你如何弹吉他，而是教你如何在游戏中使用吉他形状的控制器。 在正确的时间按下按钮是一种技能吗？ 是的！ 但这是一种不可转让的技能，不适用于实际的乐器。 该游戏的游戏机制与吉他的机制没有任何有意义的联系。它不会教你音阶或和弦，也不会教你如何以新的、意想不到的方式将它们组合在一起，创造出原创的东西。 在《吉他英雄》中，你所能做的就是按照游戏制作者希望的方式使用控制器，及时播放他们选择的歌曲，以获得他们指定的积分和成就。

当然，这一切都是游戏化的、有趣的，甚至令人上瘾，但最终玩家不会获得任何外部的、可转移的技能。 为此，您必须放下控制器，拿起一把真正的吉他，然后开始另一个完全不同的旅程。 也许某些《吉他英雄》玩家会这样做或愿意，这真是太棒了。 这意味着在某些时候他们对假装弹吉他、遵循别人的规则和设置不满意。 实际上，他们仍然从零开始。 有一个全新的技能树需要学习，除了控制器的形状之外，它与游戏关系不大。

作为一名《吉他英雄》玩家过去没有——现在也没有！ ——等同于吉他手。

那么，让我们回到“人工智能”，在本例中是“生成性‘人工智能’”，这种人工智能为大多数面向消费者的“人工智能”提供动力，比如 ChatGPT、Gemini、Claude 或 Grok。 与《吉他英雄》一样，生成“AI”拥有庞大的艺术家作品数据库可供借鉴（但与《吉他英雄》不同的是，《吉他英雄》的制作者获得了作品许可并向音乐家和词曲作者提供补偿，大多数生成“AI”训练数据都是盗版且无偿的）。 与《吉他英雄》一样，生成“AI”是由其制作者编程的；它的输出或多或少是由那些制造者通过算法和权重塑造的，这就是为什么 Anthropic 的 Claude “AI” 具有与“Grok”不同的“个性”，也是为什么“AI”文本和图像具有特定的色调和纹理，当你看到足够多的时候，很容易就能识别出来。 就像《吉他英雄》一样，“AI”玩起来很有趣，而且结果也很酷，至少表面上是这样。 精心调整的提示可以创造一些最初令人印象深刻的结果。

但是，就像《吉他英雄》一样，没有获得或发展任何外部创造性技能。 每个结果都是独立于项目范围内的，其所有者有自己的目标和议程，并且几乎所有利益都归于他们。 如果“AI”生成的材料纯粹由“AI”生成，则提示者不能拥有该材料，甚至作品中部分“AI”生成也会引发有关权利和所有权的法律问题。 从非常真实的意义上来说，“人工智能”甚至无法直接控制——提示是与“人工智能”的底层权重和算法的接口，由其他人选择和指导。 提示越精细，底层“人工智能”就越能使用其权重和算法来满足请求，但最终，你仍然会得到你所得到的。 如果这不完全是你想要的，你就必须希望另一个提示能让它更接近。 你不断地按下自动煎饼机上的按钮，希望它能做出你想要的煎饼。

提示就像使用 Guitar Hero 控制器一样，不会教您如何做其他事情。 提示并不能让人最终掌握坐在键盘前写短篇故事或长篇小说的技能。 它并不赋予人演奏乐器的能力。 它不会让你拿起笔来画画。 所有这些所需的技能——更不用说与他们一起创造意义的生活经历——都存在于其他地方。 当你使用“人工智能”时，你无法从这里到达那里。 你必须从零开始。 你花在“人工智能”上的时间不计入这个范围，除非是在非常有限的意义上向你展示你不想要的东西。

就像擅长《吉他英雄》并不能让一个人成为一名吉他手一样，能够提示并不能让一个人轻易成为一名创作者。 充其量，它告诉你本质上是一个统计引擎，你希望它根据它所提取的其他人工作的庞大数据库输出什么。 它拼凑在一起的任何东西都无法给你带来创造的体验。 “AI”飞轮曲柄的唯一好处是拥有“AI”的公司。 图像、音乐、视频或文本都不是来自您，这只是您要求的东西。 你不是创造者。 您也许是创作者的经理。

而且，看，对于某些人来说这就足够了！ 大量Facebook用户在他们的信息流中充斥着“人工智能”猫的图像和视频，这是有原因的（以及为什么，相当不那么可爱的是，大批机器人在这些相同的信息流中充斥着提示者希望你讨厌的人的虚假图像）。 很多人不想在任何有意义的世界意义上具有“创造力”，他们只是想要那些猫喝咖啡或其他什么的图像。 也不是所有玩过《吉他英雄》的人都想真正弹吉他。 很好（嗯，对于《吉他英雄》来说。 “人工智能”无论如何使用，都需要处理资源和权利问题。 但我相信我们都明白我要去哪里）。

但如果你想创造，它就会帮助你创造。 你不能只是提示自己进入它。 你必须这么做。 你必须学习、工作、培养技能和能力。 在你能擅长它之前，你必须先做得不好。 你的创造力必须是固有的和便携的，无论你走到哪里，你都随身携带的东西，而不是取决于亿万富翁提供的服务，而亿万富翁对服务的运作方式有自己的看法。

因为，除其他外，谁能说这些“人工智能”会存在多久？ 《吉他英雄》的最后一期已于十多年前问世。 该游戏的在线版本于 2020 年关闭。 每个曾经在《吉他英雄》中拥有疯狂技能的人都已经将这些技能搁置了一段时间了。 现在，显然今年晚些时候将推出吉他英雄概念的更新版本，这很酷，我希望它和以前的版本一样有趣。 我们会看看它能持续多久。 与此同时，只要他们的手指和肩膀坚持下去，每个学过吉他的人仍然拥有这些技能和使用它们的能力。

因此，在开始自我表达之旅时请记住这一点。 这里有一大堆路可以走。 有些会比其他的更难并且需要更多的时间。 但这些更有可能让你到达你想去的地方，培养技能和能力，让你说出你想说的话，用你想说的方式，而不必依赖任何人或任何其他东西来实现它。 您的选择！ 选好。

— JS
